items.prompt: What is the halo effect?
choices: An early impression shading later evidence
Choosing the candidate who speaks the longest
Scoring every candidate exactly the same
items.explanation: It is about impressions, not about length or sameness.

items.prompt: An interviewer likes a candidate in the first minute. What is most likely to happen to a vague answer later?
choices: It gets flagged as a red flag
It gets ignored entirely
It gets read as confident
items.explanation: The early liking tilts the reading of ambiguous evidence generously.

items.prompt: Which situation is the halo effect?
choices: Two interviewers ask different questions by accident
A warm opening makes a vague answer sound deep
A rubric lists what a 5 requires
items.explanation: Only the first is an early impression coloring a later reading.

items.prompt: Can the halo effect work in a negative direction?
choices: Yes, it can deflate good answers too
No, it only ever inflates scores
No, it only applies to written tests
items.explanation: The effect works in both directions.

items.prompt: Does an interviewer usually notice the halo effect acting on them?
choices: Yes, they feel themselves picking favorites
Yes, but only when tired or rushed
No, it feels like simply noticing things
items.explanation: It shapes small choices without feeling like a choice.

items.prompt: A teacher thinks a student is brilliant, and a vague oral answer sounds deep. What is this?
choices: A structured exam in action
The halo effect, outside hiring
A well-written rubric anchor
items.explanation: Same mechanism, different setting.

items.prompt: Which evidence is most at risk from the halo effect?
choices: Answers that could be read two ways
A clearly correct numerical result
A candidate's printed name on the sheet
items.explanation: Clear evidence leaves little room for tilting.

items.prompt: In the opening scene, the written feedback matched the 90-second impression. What does that suggest?
choices: The interview was perfectly objective
The candidate repeated their opening
Later minutes may only confirm it
items.explanation: Matching feedback hints that later minutes added little.

items.prompt: Two candidates give equally strong answers. The interviewer liked the first one at hello and was unsure about the second. Which outcome best fits the halo effect?
choices: The first is called confident, the second hesitant
Both answers receive the same score from the interviewer
The second wins because the answers decided it
The first is called rushed, the second careful
items.explanation: The same quality gets different readings depending on the opening feeling, so the first gets the generous word and the second the harsh one.
items.reference:
Halo effect in an interview
first 90 s: impression forms
later answers: read through it
ambiguous answer: generous or harsh
Why: an early impression quietly decides how every later, ambiguous piece of evidence gets read.
items.learnMore:
The halo effect

The halo effect is an early impression coloring everything after it. It matters most where evidence is ambiguous, because that is where the reading can go either way.

Common mistake

Assuming it only affects dislike. A warm first impression inflates scores just as a cool one deflates them.
items.reflection: Think of a time a strong first impression of someone changed how you read something they did later. What would you have thought of the same act from a stranger?

items.prompt: An interviewer insists their final score was based only on answers. What is the weakest part of that claim?
choices: They did not record every word the candidate said aloud
They interviewed the candidate for too short a time
They used a numeric scale instead of a letter grade
Their impression may have shaped how answers were read
items.explanation: The claim ignores that interpretation of an ambiguous answer is where the halo effect operates, so answer-based scoring can still be tilted.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT an example of the halo effect?
choices: A candidate's good school makes a weak answer look strong
A cool handshake makes a clear answer feel less sure
A candidate ranks low after getting a harder question
A friendly start makes a long pause read as thoughtfulness
items.explanation: Getting a harder question is a fairness issue about unequal questions; the others are early impressions altering how evidence is read.

items.prompt: What makes an interview structured?
choices: A longer list of questions asked in any order
Same core questions and a standard fixed beforehand
A friendly tone that puts the candidate at ease
items.explanation: Structure is about fixed questions and fixed standards.

items.prompt: In an unstructured interview, when is 'a good answer' usually decided?
choices: After hearing it, often by gut feel
Before any candidate walks in the door
By a vote of the whole company staff
items.explanation: That is exactly the weakness of unstructured interviews.

items.prompt: Why are scores from unstructured interviews hard to compare?
choices: They always use different number scales
Interviewers refuse to write anything down
Each candidate took a different interview
items.explanation: Different questions and standards break the comparison.

items.prompt: Two oral exams: one student gets easy questions, one gets hard ones. Are the grades comparable?
choices: Yes, a grade is a grade
No, the questions were not the same
Yes, as long as the teacher is friendly
items.explanation: Same questions plus same criteria is what makes grades comparable.

items.prompt: Which is a structured-interview feature?
choices: Every candidate gets the same required questions
Questions are invented as the talk flows on
The standard is chosen after the interview ends
items.explanation: Only the first is fixed in advance for all.

items.prompt: Can an interviewer ask any follow-up in a structured interview?
choices: No, follow-ups are forbidden entirely always
Yes, and the core can differ per candidate
Yes, if the required core stays the same
items.explanation: Follow-ups probe the answer; the core is shared.

items.prompt: When does the standard for a good answer get set in a structured interview?
choices: Right after the best candidate answers
Before any candidate is interviewed
At the end, once all are done
items.explanation: Fixing it first keeps the standard from bending to a favorite.

items.prompt: What does structure mainly protect against?
choices: Impressions silently deciding the score
Candidates preparing for the interview
Interviews running over their time slot
items.explanation: Its purpose is guarding the score against hidden tilt.

items.prompt: A team interviews three candidates, each with different improvised questions, then ranks them by gut feel. What is the main flaw?
choices: The interviews were all too long to be compared
The rankings compare three different interviews
Gut feel is never useful when judging any person
Three candidates is too few for any ranking at all
items.explanation: With no shared questions or standard, differences in scores may come from the interview rather than the person.
items.reference:
Same interview or different?
unstructured: questions differ per candidate
structured: same core questions for all
standard fixed before anyone is seen
Why: scores are only comparable if every candidate answered the same questions against the same standard.
items.learnMore:
Structured vs. unstructured interviews

A structured interview fixes the core questions and the standard for a good answer before any candidate is seen. That is what makes two scores comparable.

Common mistake

Thinking structure means reading from a script with no follow-ups. Follow-ups are fine; the required core stays the same.
items.reflection: Think of a comparison you made between two people or options that were each assessed differently. What would you have changed to make it fair?

items.prompt: Which change would make an interview process MORE structured?
choices: Writing the questions and scoring guide before booking anyone
Letting each interviewer choose their own favorite topic
Shortening each interview so there is less to read through
Asking the hiring manager to review every answer afterwards
items.explanation: Structure comes from fixing questions and standard before seeing candidates, not from length, preference or review.

structured: same core questions for all
standard fixed before anyone is seen

items.prompt: An interviewer follows the same five required questions but adds a follow-up when an answer is unclear. Is the interview still structured?
choices: No, any follow-up makes it unstructured once again
No, structure forbids asking about unclear points
Yes, but only if the follow-up is the same for all
Yes, the shared core is intact and follow-ups probe
items.explanation: Follow-ups that probe what was said do not break the shared core; structure is about the required questions and standard.

standard fixed before anyone is seen

items.prompt: What is an anchor in a scoring rubric?
choices: The first candidate's score used as a baseline
The interviewer's overall impression of fit
A concrete description of what a score needs
items.explanation: An anchor makes a number mean something specific.

items.prompt: Which is the better anchor for a 5?
choices: An excellent, impressive answer all round
Names a trade-off and a way to check it
The answer felt confident and well paced
items.explanation: Observable content beats a feeling.

items.prompt: When must anchors be written?
choices: Before any candidate is interviewed
After seeing the strongest answer
After the first round of feedback
items.explanation: Anchors written afterward only justify a forming score.

items.prompt: What goes wrong with 'rate 1 to 5 for problem-solving' and nothing else?
choices: The scale is too short to be useful
Candidates cannot see their own scores
A 5 means whatever the gut says
items.explanation: Without anchors the numbers hide the same subjectivity.

items.prompt: What is a trade-off, in the sample anchor?
choices: A mistake the candidate corrects
A choice that has a cost
A question the interviewer skips
items.explanation: For example, targeted logging instead of repeated redeploys.

items.prompt: What does 'validate' mean in the anchor for a 5?
choices: Check the result with evidence
Agree with the interviewer's view
Repeat the answer more slowly
items.explanation: It means evidence, not a feeling that it sounds right.

items.prompt: Who benefits from a rubric with concrete anchors?
choices: Only candidates who speak confidently
Only the interviewer who wrote it
Candidates, who are judged on content
items.explanation: Content-based scoring is fairer to quieter candidates too.

items.prompt: A rubric's 1-row says 'jumps to a fix without identifying the problem'. Is that observable?
choices: No, it depends on the candidate's mood
Yes, you can see it in the answer
No, only the interviewer's gut can tell
items.explanation: It describes something that is visible in what was said.

items.prompt: Two rubrics are proposed for the same question. Which one is genuinely anchored?
choices: 5 means a thoughtful and impressive answer overall, start to finish
5 means the best answer we hear across all of the candidates
5 means the answer names a trade-off and a way to verify it
5 means the answer felt right to the person interviewing
items.explanation: Only the first describes observable content; the others depend on feeling or on who else happens to be interviewed.
items.reference:
Number with and without anchor
'5 = excellent': a feeling
'5 = trade-off + way to check': observable
written before any candidate
Why: an anchor ties a score to something observable in the answer, so a number cannot mean whatever the interviewer feels.
items.learnMore:
Rubric anchors

A rubric describes what each score looks like for a question. An anchor is a concrete, observable line in it, decided before any candidate is interviewed.

Common mistake

Writing '1 to 5' with labels like 'poor' and 'great'. Those labels are still gut feelings.
items.reflection: Think of a grading or rating you have received. Were the levels concretely described in advance, and how did that change how fair it felt?

items.prompt: A rubric reads '3: reasonable approach, no trade-offs'. A candidate gives a polished talk with no trade-off. What is the correct use of the rubric?
choices: Score a 5, since the polish shows strong experience and skill
Score a 3, since polish cannot supply a trade-off
Score a 1, since the talk avoided discussing any costs
Hold the score until comparing with later candidates seen
items.explanation: The anchor decides what is required; delivery cannot stand in for missing content.

items.prompt: Why is an anchor written after hearing the best answer a problem?
choices: It bends to justify a score already forming
It will always be longer than a fair one would be
It makes later candidates impossible to interview
It stops the rubric from using numbers at all
items.explanation: Anchors fixed after the fact reflect what one favorite did, so they bend toward the impression instead of constraining it.

items.prompt: Why does 'try to be objective' not fix the halo effect?
choices: The effect acts through unnoticed choices
Interviewers rarely want to be objective at all
Objectivity is impossible to define in any setting
items.explanation: Intent does not reach unnoticed choices.

items.prompt: Which is a small choice the halo effect can shape?
choices: Which day of the week the interview is held
Which font the rubric is printed in
Which follow-up question feels natural
items.explanation: Follow-ups and readings are where it quietly acts.

items.prompt: An interviewer sincerely believes they were fair. What does that show about the halo effect?
choices: That the halo effect did not occur at all
Nothing, since it works without being noticed
That the interviewer is lying about it
items.explanation: Sincerity and unnoticed bias can coexist.

items.prompt: Which fix works without relying on the interviewer's awareness?
choices: Fixed questions and a written rubric
A reminder email saying 'be fair'
A longer break before each interview
items.explanation: Structure is built into the process, not the person.

items.prompt: With the candidate they like, an interviewer asks a warm follow-up. With another, a hard one. What is this?
choices: A normal, neutral way of interviewing
A rubric anchor being applied
The halo effect shaping follow-ups
items.explanation: Different follow-ups come from different feelings.

items.prompt: Why is it a problem that bias feels like 'just noticing'?
choices: It makes interviews run noticeably longer
No decision is felt, so none is re-examined
It makes candidates less willing to answer
items.explanation: If no choice is felt, none gets re-examined.

items.prompt: What does a sincere interviewer gain from structure?
choices: A check that does not rely on self-awareness
Permission to stop paying attention
A guarantee of hiring the best person
items.explanation: It adds protection that does not depend on noticing.

items.prompt: What is the weakness of 'we train interviewers to be aware'?
choices: Training is always too expensive to run
Interviewers dislike being trained at all
Awareness does not make the unnoticed visible
items.explanation: Knowing a bias exists does not reveal it in the moment.

items.prompt: A company responds to biased interviews with a memo reminding everyone to be objective. Why is this likely insufficient?
choices: Memos are never read by anyone in practice at companies
Objectivity is a quality only some people have by nature
The memo should have been sent after the interviews ended
It leaves the unnoticed mechanism in place
items.explanation: The bias acts through unnoticed choices, so a reminder changes intent without changing the process that produces the scores.
items.reference:
Intent vs. mechanism
intent: 'I will be fair'
mechanism: follow-ups and readings shift quietly
fix: build it into the process
Why: the halo effect works through small unnoticed choices, so only a structure that does not rely on noticing can remove it.
items.learnMore:
Why trying harder does not work

Wanting to be fair does not switch off the halo effect, because it acts through choices the interviewer does not experience as choices. Structure works because it does not depend on self-awareness.

Common mistake

Treating sincerity as evidence of objectivity. A sincere interviewer feels objective whether or not the bias is acting.
items.reflection: Think of a bias or habit you know you have despite wanting not to. What process or checklist, rather than willpower, could compensate for it?

items.prompt: Interviewer X says 'I never let first impressions affect me.' Which response is most accurate?
choices: Believe them, since they know their own mind best of all
Doubt them, since nobody can control impressions at all
Their confidence cannot be checked, as the bias would feel the same
Ask them to try harder on the very next candidate they see
items.explanation: Because the effect is unnoticed, self-report is not evidence; the process has to carry the protection.

fix: build it into the process

items.prompt: Which of these changes protects against the halo effect even for a well-meaning interviewer?
choices: Having the interviewer take a short mindfulness break first
Scoring each answer against anchors written beforehand
Switching the order in which the candidates are seen in
Asking the interviewer to explain their gut feeling aloud
items.explanation: Anchors fix what counts before the impression forms; the others leave the mechanism untouched.

items.prompt: Why must all candidates get the same core questions?
choices: So candidates can prepare their answers together
Scores then answer the same challenge
So interviews finish at exactly the same time
items.explanation: A shared question is what makes scores comparable.

items.prompt: Candidate A is quietly given an easier question. What happens to their rubric score?
choices: It may match B's score without B's achievement
It is automatically lowered by the rubric
It is hidden until the final round
items.explanation: Equal numbers on unequal questions mislead.

items.prompt: Is a fixed core the same as banning follow-ups?
choices: Yes, nothing may be added at all
Yes, except for the opening greeting
No, follow-ups probe the answer given
items.explanation: Follow-ups are fine; the required core is what is fixed.

items.prompt: Who could gently soften a question for a favorite candidate?
choices: Only an interviewer who dislikes the whole company
An interviewer who already likes them
Only the candidate, by asking for hints
items.explanation: The halo effect can shape the questions themselves.

items.prompt: What does a fixed core do for the interviewer?
choices: Removes the chance to set a favorite up to shine
Lets them skip reading the rubric
Guarantees every candidate scores the same
items.explanation: It limits where unnoticed favoritism can enter.

items.prompt: Two students get different oral-exam questions. What is wrong with ranking them?
choices: Oral exams cannot be ranked at all
Students must answer in the same order
The questions differ in difficulty
items.explanation: Different questions break the comparison.

items.prompt: Is a well-anchored rubric enough on its own?
choices: Yes, anchors fix everything
No, the questions also have to match
Yes, if the interviewers are experienced
items.explanation: Anchors plus shared questions are both needed.

items.prompt: What should follow-ups do in a structured interview?
choices: Probe what the candidate actually said
Hint toward the answer the interviewer hopes for
Replace the required questions entirely
items.explanation: Probing follows the answer rather than steering it.

items.prompt: Both candidates earned a 5 under the same rubric, but A was asked a simpler version of the question. What can you conclude?
choices: The 5s are not comparable as evidence of equal ability
A is the stronger candidate because the rubric says so
B is the stronger candidate because they answered less
Nothing is wrong, since the rubric words were the same
items.explanation: Identical anchor wording cannot repair different question difficulty; the scores no longer measure the same thing.
items.reference:
Rubric needs the same question
A: easier question, scores 5
B: harder question, scores 5
same number, not the same achievement
Why: a rubric only compares answers to the same question, so unequal questions make equal scores mean different things.
items.learnMore:
Why the questions must be the same too

Even a perfect rubric cannot compare answers to different questions. A fixed core stops the interviewer from quietly setting favorites up to shine.

Common mistake

Believing a good rubric alone is enough. Without shared questions, the same score can reflect different difficulty.
items.reflection: Where have you seen two people judged on tasks of different difficulty and then compared on one number? How did it feel to the person with the harder task?

items.prompt: An interviewer prefers to 'read the room' and adapt the main question to each candidate. What is the cost?
choices: The interview will usually run longer than planned
Candidates will find the questions too easy
The rubric will become impossible to print
Candidates no longer answer the same challenge
items.explanation: Adapting the core by candidate reintroduces unequal difficulty, so scores stop being comparable.

items.prompt: Which practice is consistent with a fixed core?
choices: Everyone gets different questions chosen to suit each person
Interviewers choose the core after meeting the candidate
Everyone gets five shared questions, with follow-ups on their own answers
The core is shortened for candidates who seem nervous
items.explanation: A shared required core with answer-driven follow-ups keeps comparability; the others let the impression adjust difficulty.

items.prompt: Does a rubric make the interviewer stop liking some candidates?
choices: Yes, it removes all personal feelings completely
Yes, it replaces feelings with a number
No, it keeps the liking out of the score
items.explanation: Feelings remain; only their route into the score is cut.

items.prompt: Where can a general impression go in a structured process?
choices: Folded quietly into the competency score
In a separate, labeled note
Nowhere, it must be forgotten
items.explanation: Separating keeps it visible and auditable.

items.prompt: Who decides how much weight a separate note carries?
choices: The process, in advance
Whichever candidate is liked most
The interviewer after the final answer
items.explanation: The weight should be agreed before the interviews.

items.prompt: What should 'team fit' NOT mean?
choices: Can explain a trade-off respectfully
Works through disagreement
'I enjoyed talking with them'
items.explanation: Fit needs observable criteria, not enjoyment.

items.prompt: What is a better 'team fit' criterion?
choices: Reminds me of the people I like the most
Explains a trade-off respectfully when challenged
Laughs at the interviewer's jokes and stories
items.explanation: Observable behavior beats similarity or charm.

items.prompt: Why not ban all impression notes?
choices: The impression still forms, now hidden
Notes always make interviews take longer
Candidates have the right to read all notes
items.explanation: Banning removes the only place it could be audited.

items.prompt: The competency score should answer which question?
choices: How did I feel while the candidate spoke?
Who would be the most fun to sit near?
What did the answer contain, per the anchors?
items.explanation: It is a content measure.

items.prompt: Candidate A's style was likable; B's answer was stronger. Where does the likable style belong?
choices: Added to the competency score as a bonus
In a separate note, not the competency score
Left out and denied having occurred
items.explanation: Keep different evidence in labeled places.

items.prompt: A hiring panel allows 'communicated warmly' as a separate note with an agreed small weight. Compared to a ban on all impression notes, this approach is:
choices: Less structured, since it admits that feelings exist at all
More structured, since the impression stays visible and bounded
Equal, since both end up in a final decision anyway
More biased, since notes would always override the scores
items.explanation: Keeping the impression in its own labeled place with a pre-agreed weight stops it hiding in the score and keeps it auditable.
items.reference:
Keep each kind of evidence in its place
competency score: content vs anchors
separate note: other observations
weight agreed in advance
Why: structure keeps impressions out of the competency score without pretending they do not exist.
items.learnMore:
Impressions do not disappear

A rubric stops an impression from silently becoming the competency score. Other observations can live in a separate, labeled place with a weight decided beforehand. 'Team fit' needs observable criteria, not 'I liked them'.

Common mistake

Banning all impressions from the record. They still form, and now they are invisible instead of auditable.
items.reflection: Think of a decision where liking someone and judging their work got mixed. How could you have kept the two in separate columns?

items.prompt: A reviewer marks a candidate down for 'poor team fit', explaining 'we just didn't click.' What is the best response?
choices: Ask for an observable behavior tied to a defined criterion
Accept it, since fit is naturally a gut matter for people
Raise the competency score to even things out later on
Drop the criterion because it is far too subjective to use
items.explanation: 'Didn't click' is an impression; fit counts only if tied to criteria defined beforehand that can be seen in the interview.

items.prompt: After structure is introduced, an interviewer still prefers Candidate A's company. Which statement is correct?
choices: That means the structure has failed and must be redone
That proves the rubric anchors were far too lenient
That means the interviewer is not suited to interviewing
Expected; the rubric only limits its route into the score
items.explanation: Structure does not erase preferences; it limits their route into the part of the decision that should rest on content.
items.reference:
Keep each kind of evidence in its place
competency score: content vs anchors
separate note: other observations
weight agreed in advance
Why: structure keeps impressions out of the competency score without pretending they do not exist.
items.learnMore:
Impressions do not disappear

A rubric stops an impression from silently becoming the competency score. Other observations can live in a separate, labeled place with a weight decided beforehand. 'Team fit' needs observable criteria, not 'I liked them'.

Common mistake

Banning all impressions from the record. They still form, and now they are invisible instead of auditable.

items.prompt: In the worked case, what score did Candidate A get against the rubric?
items.explanation: A reasonable but generic answer with no trade-off.

items.prompt: In the worked case, what score did Candidate B get against the rubric?
items.explanation: B named a trade-off and a way to check.

items.prompt: What decided the unstructured outcome?
choices: The rubric anchors
The early impression
The length of each answer
items.explanation: No anchors existed to say otherwise.

items.prompt: What did the unstructured written feedback describe?
choices: Delivery, such as 'strong communicator'
Content, such as the trade-off that was named
Nothing, since no feedback was ever written
items.explanation: It talked about manner, not substance.

items.prompt: Which element of B's answer earned the higher score?
choices: A quiet speaking style throughout
A longer pause before answering
A stated trade-off and a way to check
items.explanation: Anchors reward content.

items.prompt: What did the interviewer likely keep after the rubric was added?
choices: A new dislike of Candidate A overall
Their personal preference for A
A belief that both answers were identical
items.explanation: Preferences remain, apart from the score.

items.prompt: Did the answers change between the two versions?
choices: No, only the way they were scored
Yes, both candidates improved them
Yes, the question was easier
items.explanation: The comparison holds the answers fixed.

items.prompt: What does the demo show at a 50% weight on first impression?
choices: B leads by two points
A leads by two points
A and B tie
items.explanation: At 50% the rubric lead exactly cancels.

items.prompt: In the demo model, B leads A by 2 - 4w points. At which weight on first impression do they tie?
items.explanation: Setting 2 - 4w = 0 gives w = 0.5.
items.reference:
Same two answers, scored two ways
unstructured: A looks stronger
structured: A = 3, B = 5
the answers did not change
Why: the answers stayed identical; only the scoring process changed, and it flipped who looked stronger.
items.learnMore:
Same answers, two outcomes

In the worked case, A's fluent but generic answer scored 3 and B's halting but specific answer scored 5 once anchors forced the evaluator to find content. The written record also shifts from describing delivery to describing content.

Common mistake

Concluding that the quiet candidate always wins under structure. The rubric rewards content, whoever has it.

items.prompt: A structured process scores the same answers as the unstructured one, yet the ranking flips. What best explains the flip?
choices: The candidates changed their answers between the two versions
The rubric forced a search for content, not delivery
The structured interviewer was simply more experienced overall
The quiet candidate always wins whenever a rubric is used
items.explanation: The answers were identical; what changed was what the evaluator was required to find in them.

choices: Which answer was technically more rigorous
That the interviewer preferred the first candidate's style
That the feedback describes delivery
That the record says little about content
items.explanation: Delivery-focused feedback leaves content unrecorded, so rigor cannot be inferred either way.

items.prompt: Can a structured process still be biased?
choices: No, structure removes every kind of bias
Yes, if the rubric rewards the wrong things
No, only unstructured ones are ever biased
items.explanation: A flawed rubric makes bias consistent.

items.prompt: Which is a rubric design check?
choices: Does it measure something the job needs?
Is it printed on high-quality paper stock?
Is it shorter than the interview itself?
items.explanation: Relevance to the job is the first check.

items.prompt: Why must an anchor be observable?
choices: Otherwise candidates cannot read it properly
Otherwise it takes much longer to print out
Otherwise scoring becomes guesswork
items.explanation: Unobservable criteria bring back gut feel.

items.prompt: A rubric rewards one specific incident type. Who does that favor?
choices: Candidates with the quietest delivery style
Candidates who saw a similar incident
Candidates with the longest answers given
items.explanation: It rewards lucky familiarity.

items.prompt: Two interviewers read the same anchor differently. What does that suggest?
choices: The anchor is ambiguous and needs rewriting
One of the interviewers should be removed from it
The candidate answered unclearly in the room
items.explanation: Anchors should read the same to different people.

items.prompt: Who should review a rubric before it is used?
choices: Only its author
Only the most senior interviewer
More than one person
items.explanation: Several reviewers catch blind spots.

items.prompt: What happens with a consistent but irrelevant rubric?
choices: Scores are random and unusable by anyone
Scores are comparable yet miss what matters
Scores become fairer to every candidate
items.explanation: Consistency alone does not give validity.

items.prompt: Does structure remove the need to design the rubric well?
choices: No, design is its own task
Yes, structure takes care of it
Yes, if the rubric uses numbers
items.explanation: Structure shifts where the care is needed.

items.prompt: A rubric scores candidates on whether they mention one specific tool the team happens to use. Which design check does it fail most clearly?
choices: It is not observable in an answer at all
It cannot be printed on a single page of paper
It uses a numeric scale instead of any words at all
It rewards familiarity, not general skill
items.explanation: Naming one tool rewards lucky exposure instead of ability to solve the problem, failing the generality check.
items.reference:
Rubric design checks
needed for the job?
observable in an answer?
general skill, not one familiar incident?
same reading by two interviewers?
Why: structure removes interviewer-to-interviewer variation but a flawed rubric turns the bias into a consistent one.
items.learnMore:
When the rubric itself is flawed

A badly designed rubric produces outcomes that are consistent, comparable and still biased. Check relevance, observability, generality and agreement between readers.

Common mistake

Treating the rubric as neutral once written. It encodes choices about what counts, and those need review.
items.reflection: Think of a standard you have seen that was applied consistently but measured the wrong thing. What check would have caught it?

items.prompt: Two trained interviewers apply the same anchor to the same answer and get a 2-point gap. What is the best next step?
choices: Average the two scores together and simply move on from it
Replace whichever interviewer gave the lower score of the two
Rewrite the anchor so its requirement is more concrete
Add a third question to the interview to settle the matter
items.explanation: A wide gap points to an ambiguous anchor; sharper wording is the structural fix.

items.prompt: A team argues: 'we use a rubric, so our hiring is unbiased.' Which reply is most accurate?
choices: Correct, a rubric always removes bias completely and for good
The rubric can encode bias, so check its content too
Incorrect, because rubrics are always more biased than gut feel
Correct, provided the rubric uses a five-point scale only
items.explanation: A rubric removes interviewer variation but not bias built into what it rewards.
